title: Taking the light
hook: Krishna eats Sudama's handful of rice; why the arti flame comes back to everyone
carry: what you offer comes back as grace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hari, the one who takes the trouble away: the elephant called, and Vishnu came. Your line named him.
screen: `HARI — THE ONE WHO TAKES THE TROUBLE AWAY.`

segments.voice: A poor man stands outside a palace gate in Dvaraka, holding a small bundle of flattened rice tied in a rag. His wife begged it from the neighbors. Inside lives Krishna, his old friend from school, now a king. Who brings a handful of rice to a king? But the gates open, and Krishna runs out, hugs him, washes his feet, and sits him on his own bed. Then he smiles and asks: so, what did you bring me?
screen: `A POOR MAN AT A PALACE GATE.` → `A HANDFUL OF RICE IN A RAG.` → `WHAT DID YOU BRING ME?`

segments.voice: The friend is usually called Sudama, and the story is in the Bhagavata Purana. Sudama hides the bundle. He's ashamed. Krishna takes it from him anyway, opens it, and eats a handful with delight, as if it were the best food in the palace. In the telling, he says he gladly accepts even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, when it's offered with love. Sudama walks home without asking for a thing. When he gets there, his hut has become a house full of plenty. He gave a handful. It came back as grace. Hindus have a word for what comes back: prasad, grace. You met it with the laddus: food is offered at the shrine, then shared out as a blessing. Arti works the same way, with light. When the song ends, the lamp that was just circled before the divine is carried out to everyone. You cup your hands over the flame, close enough for warmth, never touching, then bring your hands to your eyes, your face, sometimes over your head. That's taking the light: receiving the blessing back. A few customs travel with it. An arti flame usually isn't blown out; blowing on a sacred flame is often seen as disrespectful. And if you're a guest and unsure, watch first, then copy the person beside you. The light is offered to everyone in the room, the way Krishna treated a poor friend's handful as a king's gift.
screen: `KRISHNA EATS THE RICE WITH DELIGHT.` · `PRASAD: WHAT COMES BACK IS GRACE.` · `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, THEN TO THE EYES.` · `DON'T BLOW IT OUT.`

segments.voice: If it's safe, light a candle or lamp; if not, picture the arti plate coming toward you. Cup your hands and pass them slowly over the warmth, a few inches above, never touching, then draw them back and rest your palms softly over your closed eyes, feeling the warmth there. Once more, and this time let your hands pass over the top of your head, then rest them in your lap and stay with the flame.
Jyoti, the flame: after arti it comes back out to the people, and hands pass over it to the eyes and the head, taking the light as grace. Today's word.
Your line: what you offer comes back as grace. Sudama gave a handful; the light comes back to your hands. Until tomorrow.

screen: `WHAT YOU OFFER COMES BACK AS GRACE.` → `DAY 121 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FAMILY ARTI.`

howItsDone: At the end of arti, the lamp is brought to each person, who passes cupped hands over the flame without touching it and then touches the hands to the eyes, face or head; in temples, people often place a small offering on the plate as it passes.
